queries.hook: I feel like an imposter. Inside, my mind won't settle, and I don't know how to carry it.

queries.steady: A mistake is something you did, not who you are; no one who tries to do good is ever lost.
queries.act: Be on your own side: lift yourself up, make amends where you can, and begin again; no one who does good is lost.

hook.speaker: Vibhishan
hook.setting: Vibhishan, Ravana's good-hearted brother, describes his life in Ravana's court.
hook.sanskrit: सुनहु पवनसुत रहनि हमारी। जिमि दसनन्हि महुँ जीभ बिचारी॥ तात कबहुँ मोहि जानि अनाथा। करिहहिं कृपा भानुकुल नाथा ॥
hook.line: I live here like the tongue among the teeth.
hook.translation: Son of the wind, hear how I live: like the poor tongue among the teeth. Friend, knowing me to be without support, will the Lord of the Sun dynasty ever show me grace?
hook.why: Even in a hostile place there may be one ally; find them.

prasang.title: Hanuman finds a friend in Lanka
prasang.summary: Searching Lanka, Hanuman is surprised to find a house with Ram's name on it. Its owner, Vibhishan, Ravana's brother, says he lives in Lanka like a tongue among teeth. Hanuman tells him even a restless monkey like himself was given Ram's love.
prasang.story_hook: In a city of demons, Hanuman heard someone wake up and say Ram's name.
prasang.lesson: Even in a hostile place there may be one ally; find them.

alternates.ref: Mahabharata · Udyoga Parva · Udyoga: Krishna's peace embassy
alternates.speaker: Yudhishthira
alternates.setting: Before Krishna leaves for the Kaurava court, Yudhishthira lays out why he wants peace, not war.
alternates.sanskrit: अधनाद्धि निवर्तन्ते ज्ञातयः सुहृदो द्विजाः / अपुष्पादफलाद्वृक्षाद्यथा कृष्ण पतत्रिणः
alternates.line: When money runs out, some friends drift away, like birds leaving a tree with no fruit.
alternates.translation: When a man has no money, relatives, friends and brahmins turn away from him, the way birds leave a tree that has no flowers and no fruit.
alternates.why: Winning a feud still costs you peace. Hostility only ends when someone stops feeding it.

prasang.title: Yudhishthira's case for peace
prasang.summary: Before Krishna sets out as peace envoy, Yudhishthira opens his heart: poverty humiliates, greed corrodes, victory breeds enmity, and hostility is never ended by hostility. He asks only for five villages.
prasang.lesson: Winning a feud still costs you peace. Hostility only ends when someone stops feeding it.

alternates.speaker: Tulsidas
alternates.setting: Bharat walks toward Ram, slowed by shame, quickened by love.
alternates.sanskrit: फेरति मनहुँ मातु कृत खोरी। चलत भगति बल धीरज धोरी॥ जब समुझत रघुनाथ सुभाऊ। तब पथ परत उताइल पाऊ ॥
alternates.line: Shame slowed him. But whenever he remembered Ram's nature, his feet moved faster.
alternates.translation: It was as if his mother's wrong held him back, while the strength of devotion drove him on like a patient ox. Whenever he remembered Raghunath's nature, his feet moved faster on the path.

verse.speaker: Vasishtha
verse.setting: After the story of two grieving brothers, Vasishtha tells Rama how worry feeds itself.
verse.sanskrit: चिन्तनेनैधते चिन्ता त्विन्धनेनेव पावकः । नश्यत्यचिन्ततेनैव विनेन्धनमिवानलः ॥
verse.line: Worry grows when you feed it thought, like fire with fuel. Starve it, and it dies down.
verse.translation: Worry grows by thinking, as fire grows with fuel; and it dies by not being thought, as fire dies without fuel.
verse.why: Grief is love; endless rumination is the part we can learn to stop feeding.

prasang.title: Punya consoles his younger brother Pavana after their parents die
prasang.summary: Two brothers live with their parents by the Ganga. When their father and mother die, the elder, Punya, performs the rites calmly while the younger, Pavana, wanders the forest weeping. Punya gently helps him see that the bonds of 'mine' and 'not mine' are made in the mind. Vasishtha draws the lesson: worry grows when fed, and a full mind finds the world full.
prasang.story_hook: When their parents died, one brother quietly lit the funeral fires and the other ran weeping into the forest.
prasang.lesson: Grief is love; endless rumination is the part we can learn to stop feeding.

verse.for_you: Today, your mind feeds the worry that you do not belong. You do not need to feed it.
verse.try_today: Notice when worry grows and do not feed it.
verse.scene_line: Like Punya and Pavana, you stand between two worlds of thought.

why: Worry grows when you feed it (Yoga Vasishtha 5.21.6)
worry is shown to live on the attention it is fed

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: From the section praising learning, addressed to proud rulers.
verse.sanskrit: हर्तुर्याति न गोचरं किमपि शं पुष्णाति यत् सर्वदा- ऽप्यर्थिभ्यः प्रतिपाद्यमानमनिशं प्राप्नोति वृद्धिं पराम् । कल्पान्तेष्वपि न प्रयाति निधनं विद्याख्यमन्तर्धनं येषां तान् प्रति मानमुज्झत नृपाः कस्तैः सह स्पर्धते ॥
verse.line: Learning is wealth no thief can see. It grows when you give it away and never perishes.
verse.translation: It never comes within a thief's sight; it always nourishes some deep good; given to those who ask, it grows greater; even at the end of an age it does not perish. Kings, drop your pride before those who own this inner wealth called learning. Who can compete with them?
verse.why: What you learn and how you speak are the wealth no one can take from you.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: In praise of learning and the learned
prasang.summary: Bhartrihari praises learning as wealth no thief can take and speech as the one lasting ornament, then turns to good company and the three kinds of people who face obstacles. It ends with the 'sword's-edge vow' of the good.
prasang.lesson: What you learn and how you speak are the wealth no one can take from you.

verse.for_you: Yesterday, worry fed on your thoughts. Today, your learning is a wealth no thief can see. It grows when you give it away and never perishes.
verse.try_today: Give away one thing you know to someone who asks for it today.
verse.scene_line: You stand before them, and your learning grows as you share it.

why: A wealth the rich do not outrank
What one has learned cannot be taken

verse.speaker: Sage Nishakara
verse.setting: The old vulture Sampati, wings burnt and grounded for ages, is told why he should live on.
verse.sanskrit: उत्सहेयमहं कर्तुमद्यैव त्वां सपक्षकम्। इहस्थस्त्वं हि लोकानां हितं कार्यं करिष्यसि॥
verse.line: You are needed exactly where you are, as you are. Your use isn't over.
verse.translation: I could give you back your wings this very day. But by staying here as you are, you will do something for the good of the world.
verse.why: Even when you feel useless, your experience may be exactly what someone needs.

prasang.title: Sampati, the bird who could not fly
prasang.summary: The despairing monkeys meet Sampati, Jatayu's old brother, whose wings burnt long ago. A sage once told him to live on, because one day his knowledge would be needed. Now he tells them Sita is in Lanka, and his wings grow back.
prasang.story_hook: For thousands of years the old bird had sat on a mountain with no wings, waiting for a reason.
prasang.lesson: Even when you feel useless, your experience may be exactly what someone needs.

verse.for_you: Today, you are needed exactly where you are, as you are. Your use isn't over.
verse.try_today: Notice one way your presence helps in today's meeting.

why: 'Do not feel small'; someone reminds you who you are.
being grounded is not being useless

verse.speaker: Vidura
verse.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
verse.sanskrit: प्रज्ञावृद्धं धर्मवृद्धं स्वबन्धुं / विद्यावृद्धं वयसा चापि वृद्धम् / कार्याकार्ये पूजयित्वा प्रसाद्य / यः संपृच्छेन्न स मुह्येत्कदाचित्
verse.line: When unsure what to do, respectfully ask someone older and wiser. You won't go astray.
verse.translation: One who honours and wins over a kinsman mature in wisdom, in goodness, in learning and in years, and asks him what should and should not be done, is never confused.
verse.why: Don't trade what's right for desire, fear or money. Only your deeds stay with you.

prasang.title: Vidura Niti: never abandon what is right
prasang.summary: Vidura closes with the heart of his counsel: never give up what is right for desire, fear or greed; only our deeds go with us; ask the wise when unsure.
prasang.lesson: Don't trade what's right for desire, fear or money. Only your deeds stay with you.

verse.for_you: Your work is needed. You can ask a wiser kinsman when unsure. You will not go astray.
verse.try_today: Ask a trusted mentor one question about your next presentation.
verse.scene_line: You stand before your colleagues, and you ask Vidura for guidance.

verse.speaker: Vasishtha
verse.setting: A powerful king offers a fortune for the sage's cow, the source of his whole way of life.
verse.sanskrit: नाहं शतसहस्रेण नापि कोटिशतैर्गवाम्॥ राजन् दास्यामि शबलां राशिभी रजतस्य वा। न परित्यागमयं मत्सकाशादरिंदम ॥
verse.line: Not for any price. Some things are not for sale, however powerful the buyer.
verse.translation: Not for a hundred thousand cows, not for a billion, not for heaps of silver, O king, will I give up Shabala. She stays with me.
verse.why: Envy and force cannot take what someone will not give; real power is built inside.

prasang.title: The king who wanted the cow
prasang.summary: King Vishvamitra is feasted by the sage Vasishtha and covets the wish-granting cow that made it possible. Vasishtha refuses every offer; the king takes her by force and is routed, then fails again with divine weapons. Humbled, he resolves to transform himself through inner discipline instead of force.
prasang.story_hook: A king who had everything saw one thing he could not buy, and it undid him.
prasang.lesson: Envy and force cannot take what someone will not give; real power is built inside.

verse.for_you: Now you face a king with no price. Your worth is not for sale, however powerful the buyer.
verse.try_today: Notice one thing you value that no offer can buy.
verse.scene_line: You stand before the board, a king with a fortune, yet your worth is not for sale.

why: what sustains his life is not for sale
a plain no to someone far more powerful

story.title: 'Sisters and Brothers of America': Chicago, 11 September 1893
characters: Delegates and audience of the World's Parliament of Religions
story.story_hook: On 11 September 1893, a young Indian monk with no formal invitation stood up in Chicago and said five words that brought the hall to its feet.
story.summary: An unknown 30-year-old monk from India, with no invitation and little money, rises on the Parliament's opening day and greets the hall as 'Sisters and Brothers of America'. The audience stands and applauds for minutes. In a five-minute address he says India's faith accepts all religions as true and hopes the day marks the death-knell of fanaticism.
story.lesson: You can belong fully to your own tradition and still honour every other path.
story.hook_title: Vivekananda had no invitation, and five words brought Chicago to its feet
story.teaser: Vivekananda had no invitation, and five words brought Chicago to its feet
story.for_you: Your worth is not for sale. You can be unprepared and terrified and still step up.
